reason: “His heart did take courage” on receiving Pahoran's letter is close in situation to Acts 28:15, where Paul, meeting the brethren at Appii forum, “thanked God, and took courage”; the KJV has the phrase in only two verses (the other is 2 Chronicles 15:8, Asa after Oded's prophecy). But the shared string is two words of ordinary English, the Book of Mormon adds “his heart did”, which neither source has, and encouragement on the arrival of good news needs no model. Recorded because the rarity count invites the link and the count is not enough.

“He did raise the standard of liberty in whatsoever place he did enter” tempts a reader toward Isaiah's raised standard (“set up my standard to the people”, Isaiah 49:22; “lift up a standard”, Isaiah 59:19), and Isaiah 49 is a chapter the Book of Mormon transcribes entire at 1 Nephi 21. It should not be taken here. “Standard” occurs in nineteen KJV verses, most of them Numbers' tribal ensigns, and the phrase “raise the standard” occurs in none. The title of liberty is the Book of Mormon's own object, made and adjudicated at Alma 46:12 against Nehemiah 4:14 and 1 Kings 11:30; 62:4 is Moroni carrying the thing he made there.

A six-word run, and the temptation is stronger than usual because the source is the fall of Jerusalem — the event on which the whole Book of Mormon is founded — and because Zedekiah's flight, like Moroni's escalade, involves a wall at night. But the direction is opposed at every point: Zedekiah and his men of war go “forth out of the city by night” between the two walls to escape a siege, and Moroni's men are “let down into the city by night” to take one. Jeremiah 52:7 scores the same run because it is the same sentence twice. The verse's proposed source is Joshua 2:15, filed at 62:21, where the cord and the wall are, and where the same inversion of direction is the argument.

sharedText: and it came to pass that as many as
reason: A nine-word run consisting of the Book of Mormon's universal narrative opener plus “as many as”. Abner kills Asahel with the hinder end of a spear and the bystanders stand still; Moroni grants the Lamanite prisoners' request to join the people of Ammon. Nothing is shared but the connective. Covered in kind by the standing exclusion at 1 Nephi 1:5, and recorded here only because the run length is the longest in the chapter and would otherwise look like a finding.

sharedText: a javelin … he did not awake
reason: A cross-reference, not a rejection, and the second half of an argument made elsewhere. Teancum's killing of Amalickiah at Alma 51:34 is adjudicated against Jael and Sisera, and 52:1 against Judges 4:22; 62:36 is the same type-scene run a second time on Amalickiah's brother — a sleeping king, a weapon driven home by a lone assassin at night. What is new here is that it fails on the one detail Judges 4:21 insists on. Jael's Sisera “died”, without waking; Alma 51:34 keeps that, noting that Teancum “did cause the death of the king immediately, that he did not awake his servants”. At 62:36 “the king did awake his servant before he died, insomuch that they did pursue Teancum, and slew him.” The type-scene is repeated in order to be broken, and the break costs Teancum his life. Registered here so that a reader arriving at 62:36 is sent to Alma 51:34.

sharedText: gone the way of all the earth
reason: A cross-reference within the book. The formula occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Joshua 23:14 and 1 Kings 2:2, and enters the corpus at 2 Nephi 1:14 in Lehi's mouth; within Alma it is adjudicated at 1:1, of Mosiah. This is Mormon using his own inherited formula and the argument is not restated. It is worth noting what he uses it on. In both KJV verses and in every earlier Book of Mormon occurrence the phrase belongs to an old man taking leave of his people in an ordered succession — Joshua, David, Lehi, Mosiah, Alma. Teancum is stabbed to death in an enemy camp in the middle of the night while attempting a murder. The formula is applied to him anyway, in the same sentence that calls him “a true friend to liberty”, and the effect is to enrol an assassin's death among the peaceful ones.

sharedText: slew them with a great slaughter
reason: A seven-word run, and no source can be identified behind it. “With a great slaughter” occurs in eight KJV verses spread across Joshua, Judges, 1 Samuel, 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles, and it is the KJV's standard notice of a decisive field victory; four of the eight attach it to the same verb the Book of Mormon uses. The phrase is real biblical English rather than boilerplate, which is why it is registered rather than passed over, but it points at a genre and not at a verse.

“Began to multiply and to wax exceeding strong again in the land” sits close to Exodus 1:7's “multiplied, and waxed exceeding mighty; and the land was filled with them”, and the KJV has “waxed exceeding” in only two verses. The Book of Mormon's adjective is “strong”, not “mighty”, and the corpus's growth formula is already sourced elsewhere — Genesis 47:27 at Jarom 1:8 and Mosiah 2:2, Exodus 1:10 at Mosiah 9:11 — so nothing distinctive is left over for Exodus 1:7 to explain. Registered because the Exodus reading is thematically inviting at a moment when Nephite prosperity is about to turn, and because a careful reader would want to know it was considered.
